articles.title: Tech executive Shannon Burns, who slept in sauna after forgetting room key on Austria trip, can pursue £76 million from Gitpod; tribunal rejects £1 million cap amid OpenAI acquisition
articles.summary: A senior technology executive who was dismissed after sleeping in a sauna during a work trip has been given the right to pursue a £76 million compensation
articles.body: A senior technology executive who was dismissed after sleeping in a sauna during a work trip has been given the right to pursue a £76 million compensation claim against software company Gitpod, in a case that could result in one of the largest awards in British employment tribunal history.Shannon Burns can formally seek £76,071,992 after the Birmingham Employment Tribunal rejected Gitpod’s application to restrict her potential compensation claim to £1 million. The development was reported by The Independent, which said the proposed payout could surpass the current known record of £4.58 million.Burns was dismissed after Austria work tripBurns was hired by Gitpod in late 2022 as its vice-president of engineering, with an annual salary of £220,000 and a £78,000 bonus. Before joining the company, she had held positions at Silicon Valley firms including Slack and Lyft.In April 2023, she attended a team-building event in Lofer, Austria, where she and other employees, including CEO Johannes Landgraf, consumed alcohol.One evening, Burns was unable to enter her room after forgetting her key. Her ADHD, which she had disclosed to the company, was described during the tribunal proceedings as causing significant forgetfulness and a tendency to lose items. Unable to access her room, she slept in a sauna.Following the trip, Landgraf raised concerns about what he described as her “lack of professional accountability”. Burns was dismissed in June 2023.Burns later argued that her male colleagues had also been drinking during the event but that she was the only one dismissed.Tribunal found disability discriminationIn 2025, the Birmingham Employment Tribunal ruled in Burns’ favour on her claims of discrimination arising from disability and failure to make reasonable adjustments. Her separate claim of direct sex discrimination was dismissed. The tribunal ordered that a further hearing would determine compensation.Burns has ADHD and has said that she developed PTSD during the period surrounding her dismissal. She has since left the technology industry and is retraining as a therapist.Her £76 million schedule of loss is based largely on projected future earnings and lost equity. According to the case, Burns argues that she could have continued earning at a high level in the technology sector had she not been dismissed.Gitpod sought to cap the claim at £1 millionAt the latest hearing, Gitpod asked the tribunal to impose a £1,000 deposit order and effectively prevent Burns from pursuing losses above £1 million.The company described her claim for more than £76 million as “extraordinary” and argued that the calculations in her schedule of loss had “little reasonable prospect of success”.Burns’ lawyers opposed the application, describing it as “oppressive”.Employment Judge Rachel Wedderspoon rejected Gitpod’s application. She noted that Burns had an “exceptionally high pay history” and that her calculations included not only lost salary but also potential losses relating to equity.The judge said the size of the claim was “highly unusual” and potentially more typical of awards sought in the United States. However, she concluded that the tribunal could not determine at this stage that Burns’ valuation had little reasonable prospect of success without expert evidence on employment remuneration and medical matters.OpenAI acquisition could affect Burns’ sharesThe tribunal also ordered Gitpod to disclose information concerning the value of its recent sale to OpenAI.Judge Wedderspoon referred to an acquisition value believed to be $400 million (£302 million). Burns is understood to hold a 0.85 per cent stake in Gitpod.Based on that valuation, the tribunal said her shares could be worth around $3.4 million (£2.6 million), potentially rising to $27.85 million (£21 million) in four years if the $400 million figure proves accurate.OpenAI's acquisition of Gitpod, which was rebranded as Ona, has been subject to regulatory proceedings. Australian competition authorities have confirmed that the proposed acquisition involved OpenAI acquiring 100 per cent of Gitpod, Inc., known as Ona.Burns’ lawyer accuses Gitpod of delaying the caseTara Grossman, an employment lawyer assisting Burns, described the tribunal decision as a “resounding success” and defended the £76 million calculation.She said Burns had already earned more than £1 million in junior technology roles and that her Gitpod compensation package included both a £220,000 salary and equity that could potentially have become highly valuable.Grossman also accused Gitpod of using aggressive legal tactics to prolong the dispute and put pressure on Burns. She said the company’s attempt to reduce the claim to £1 million was particularly problematic because it was aware of the potential value of Burns’ Gitpod shares following the OpenAI transaction.Those assertions are Burns’ legal team's characterization of the proceedings and have not been established as findings of the tribunal.Compensation hearing is still to comeDespite the latest ruling, Burns has not been awarded £76 million.The tribunal has only ruled that she can pursue the amount claimed, while the final compensation figure will be determined at a separate remedy hearing. That hearing is expected to take place after the conclusion of the ongoing appeal proceedings relating to the earlier tribunal ruling.The tribunal’s 2025 judgment established Burns’ successful disability-related claims but left the question of compensation for a later hearing.If Burns ultimately receives an award close to the amount she is seeking, it would represent an extraordinary figure by British employment tribunal standards. The £76 million figure therefore remains a claim being pursued, rather than a sum already awarded by the tribunal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
articles.summary: Pakistan says it struck 10 targets, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".
articles.body:
Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.

The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.

Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".

It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.

In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.

Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.

In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.

In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.

"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."

Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".

Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".

Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".

The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.

A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) , which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.

Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.

Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.

Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.

Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.

Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.

The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".

The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.

During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

articles.title: Israel’s policies threaten ‘very existence’ of Palestinians, Abbas tells UN
articles.summary: Mahmoud Abbas says saving two-state solution begins with preserving Palestinian land, protecting those who live on it.
articles.body:
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has ⁠warned the United Nations General Assembly that Israel’s policies go beyond undermining a two-state solution and now threaten the “very life and existence” of Palestinians.

Abbas’s prerecorded remarks from his office in Ramallah were broadcast before the assembly on Thursday after the United States denied visas to a Palestinian delegation to attend the gathering for the second year in a row.

Abbas said Palestinians were living through one of the “most dangerous periods” of their history, citing “killing, destruction, starvation, attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe”.

He said Israeli forces were erasing Palestinian lives in Gaza.

“Neighbourhoods, cities, refugee camps, institutions, schools, universities, hospitals, mosques, and churches have been destroyed. Every foundation of life, and the future of entire generations, has been targeted.”

He called Israeli activities in the occupied West Bank a “malicious colonial plan” and said Palestinians were being pushed into forced displacement, with “realities on the ground” changing every day in reference to Israeli settlements being built on Palestinian land, a practice that is illegal under international law.

Abbas urged the international community to implement the two-state solution on the basis of international law to guarantee security.

“Saving the solution begins with preserving the land on which the Palestinian state is to be established” and protecting the people who live on it, he said.

Abbas said any transitional period must lead to the reunification of the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank under one Palestinian state with a single legitimate armed force.

Domestically, Abbas said, the Palestinian Authority plans to hold legislative elections ⁠on November 28, the first such vote in 20 years, despite doubts it will go ahead.

Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, when Hamas took control of Gaza.

“We have completed the national reform programme to which we committed ourselves before our people and the international community,” Abbas said.

Abbas’s comments came as Hamas accused Israel on Thursday of trying to derail a “ceasefire” and a process by the US-backed Board of Peace to end the war in Gaza.

Hamas agreed to a 15-point roadmap that included the disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian factions, the transfer of Gaza’s administration to a Palestinian national committee, and a phased Israeli withdrawal.

In a statement, Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said the group was “fully ready to implement the roadmap agreed with the Board of Peace concerning the peace plan in the Gaza Strip”, and had taken the measures necessary to comply with the deal.

Qassem said Israel was refusing to meet its commitments of the ceasefire deal and the Gaza roadmap while escalating attacks on Palestinians.

He added that the Board of Peace and its high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, had failed to compel Israel to implement the deal.

With both processes to end conflict in Gaza and the occupied West Bank uncertain, a two-state solution seems to be slipping further away.

articles.title: Backlash erupts over Hasan Piker’s upcoming speaking engagement at Cornell
articles.summary: Hasan Piker's Cornell University event drew sharp backlash from Hillel group on campus, which called his rhetoric "repulsive" and antisemitic ahead of his arrival.
articles.body: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has yet to take the podium at Cornell University, but he's already facing sharp backlash from critics who say his presence reflects deeper issues at the core of campus culture. The event, which is part of the "Students Not Bombs" campaign, is being hosted on Sept. 24 by the university's chapters of Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP), Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA) and Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP). Piker has a history of making controversial remarks, and famously said that America "deserved" 9/11, a statement that he later walked back and apologized for. He is also a vocal critic of Israel and U.S. foreign policy. WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS Critics have already spoken out against the event, with the university's Hillel calling Piker's commentary "repulsive" in a statement posted to social media. "The university is a place to learn, to argue, to explore, and to debate. Mr. Piker's views, however, go against our values as Americans and Jews, and his hateful, antisemitic rhetoric is repulsive," Grinspoon Hillel at Cornell said in a statement. For William Jacobson, a clinical professor and director of the Securities Law Clinic at Cornell Law School, Piker's appearance on campus is not a one-off event, rather it represents what he calls a "campaign of intimidation." "It's not really surprising to me that the anti-Israel groups on campus have invited as incendiary a speaker as Hasan Piker. In fact, it's very much in keeping with the tactics of intimidation that they've been doing really as long as I've been at Cornell — which is approaching 19 years — but which has ramped up dramatically after October 7," Jacobson told Fox News Digital. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS Jacobson cited past incidents in which conservative speakers faced disruptions, such as former U.S. senator from Pennsylvania and presidential candidate Rick Santorum, Tea Party movement co-founder Michael Johns and Ann Coulter, who is a Cornell alumna. In 2016, Santorum was heckled during an event at the university. He said that the protests at the Cornell event were demonstrating "liberal intolerance," The Cornell Daily Sun reported. The event with Johns in 2017 was made private on the advice of the Cornell University Police Department, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Jacobson recalled that, despite the event being private, protesters found out where Johns was speaking and "banged on the doors." In 2022, Coulter was forced to end her event early after several attendees protested, eight of whom were removed from the room, the outlet also reported. The student newspaper noted that when Coulter returned to the university in 2024, she did not face the same amount of disruption, but one faculty member was arrested for disorderly behavior. Cornell University did not respond to inquiries addressing Jacobson's specific comments. But in a statement to Fox News Digital regarding the controversy surrounding Piker's event, a university spokesperson emphasized that student-hosted speakers do not carry the institution's official endorsement. "Guest speakers invited by student groups undergo a thorough review to ensure an event can be hosted safely. They are not subject to an approval process around content," the university spokesperson said. "The use of spaces by student groups does not represent an endorsement or approval of, or agreement with the theme of the event or the speech of its participants. As with any event, Cornell will respond appropriately to any reports of discrimination, incitement, or disruption." CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS While Cornell University maintains that all student groups have the ability to host speakers, Jacobson argues that even the coverage surrounding the events creates a distorted narrative on campus. Jacobson criticized The Cornell Daily Sun's framing of Piker's event, saying the student newspaper's characterization of the controversial Twitch streamer as a "left-wing political commentator" was overly generous. "'The Cornell Sun' has depicted Hasan Piker as just merely a left-wing activist, and we all know that that's not what he is. He's beyond left-wing. He's incendiary," Jacobson said. "To describe him in that superficial way like The Cornell Sun [sic] did, really, I think, does a disservice to its readers, because somebody just reading that wouldn't understand why is this even controversial. And unfortunately, that's something I've seen The Cornell Sun [sic] do repeatedly with regard to the anti-Israel movement on campus — they always tone it down." When reached for comment on Jacobson's characterization of their coverage, The Cornell Daily Sun told Fox News Digital, "We appreciate the concern, and we understand that this visit matters deeply to many people in our community. A headline can only say so much, which is why we hope readers will look to our full coverage." "Our initial article discusses the controversy surrounding Mr. Piker, including his statement that 'America deserved 9/11' and his recent comments regarding Israel and American Jews. We have since published a second article sharing statements from Jewish student organizations on campus, along with further remarks by Mr. Piker and reactions from students ahead of his visit," the statement read. The student newspaper said it would "continue to report on" Piker's event and the response on campus, adding, "We truly care about getting this story right, and about making sure the students most affected by it are heard in our coverage." HASAN PIKER ADMITS HE HAS 'DIALED DOWN' HIS OPINIONS AFTER PUBLIC AND DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH Jacobson emphasized that he was not calling for the event with Piker to be canceled, rather he was hoping it would start a dialogue about escalating political polarization on campus. "In some sense, I am glad they invited him, because maybe now we can have an honest conversation on campus about how poisonous the movement is that is bringing him to campus. That's the conversation we need to have, not 'should we kick them off, should we block them,'" Jacobson told Fox News Digital. articles.title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
articles.summary: A male suspect from Ukraine was arrested after the stabbings in the town of Jarosław, police say.
articles.body:
A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.

A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil".

Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way.

Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.

The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.

Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".

Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack.

In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."

Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

articles.summary: Trump's visit to Neyland Stadium forces Steve Sarkisian, Josh Heupel to plan for communication cuts as Secret Service scrambles coach-to-player headsets.
articles.body: KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — There was already enough anticipation surrounding the upcoming showdown between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee at Neyland Stadium this weekend. Now, with President Donald Trump planning to attend Saturday’s high-stakes SEC matchup, both teams will have to prepare for circumstances beyond their control. And sure, there will be folks at home who laugh about the pictures coming from Tennessee's campus that show a large bottleneck of traffic outside the stadium. But, once again, having been a part of three college football games with the president in attendance, it's not as bad as some want to make it out to be from a congestion standpoint. As for the teams involved, there is one minor detail that could cause a few problems during the game. Communication could be cut at any time while the president is moving When asked on Thursday about any type of effects that will be presented when Donald Trump is inside Neyland Stadium on Saturday afternoon, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian pointed out one minor inconvenience. "Anytime the president changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication. They cut your headsets in terms of coach to player communication. So you have to plan for that," Sarkisian noted. Yes, this is actually a thing. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! During the 2026 CFP title game between Indiana and Miami, there were a few instances where communication was scrambled, with more of a white noise coming through the headsets along both sidelines. No, this wasn’t a major ordeal during the game, with both teams adapting during the moments in which communication ceased for a few seconds, but the concern is still valid. Either way, both Tennessee and Texas will adapt, and it shouldn’t be an issue that forces a coach to call a timeout. Will the Donald Trump make any type of appearance on College Gameday? articles.title: US rapper Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
articles.summary: Macklemore says ‘being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work’, promises to donate proceeds to Palestinian causes.
articles.body:
Grammy Award-winning rapper Macklemore has announced a string of shows in support of Palestine after he was controversially dropped from Ed Sheeran’s United States tour after speaking out against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

The 43-year-old American rapper, who has almost 40 million monthly listeners on Spotify, announced his Free Palestine Tour on Thursday, with shows set to take place in Dublin, Paris and London in late October.

Macklemore said he will be joined by other musicians and will announce their names soon. He added that US shows are currently being organised.

He said all proceeds raised from the tour will be donated to causes supporting the Palestinian people and the wider movement.

“If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years,” Macklemore said in a statement.

“There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now. It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” he continued.

“People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it.”

English punk rap duo Bob Vylan have expressed their support for the tour, responding to Macklemore’s Instagram post with a heart emoji. The British YouTuber and influencer known as Chunkz, who has more than four million followers on Instagram, also praised Macklemore.

On September 4 at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, Macklemore, who was one of Sheeran’s opening acts, expressed support for Palestine.

articles.title: After Rábida Island removed invasive rats in 2011, scientists later confirmed a native gecko alive there that had previously been known only from ancient remains
articles.summary: After eradicating invasive rodents from Rábida Island in the Galápagos, scientists discovered a native gecko species previously thought extinct. This groundbreaking find highlights the ecological impact of invasive species removal and the importance of biodiversity conservation.
articles.body: Historically, Rábida Island in the Galápagos had no records of living leaf-toed geckos, only bone remains dating back thousands of years. It was in 2011 that the Galápagos National Park and its partners were able to eradicate brown rats that invaded the island. After a year, a gecko was spotted, and more geckos were collected through expeditions carried out in 2019 and 2021. The paper, published in June 2025, came almost 14 years after the eradication. The authors suggest the removal of the rats may have helped the geckos, but it is not known how the two species interacted on Rábida Island before the rats were removed.A 499-hectare island with no gecko records except bones 5,700 to 8,540 years oldRábida, also called Jervis, is a 499-hectare island in the middle of Galápagos, located about 4.5 kilometers south of Santiago Island and 25 kilometers east of Isabela Island. There are 11 kinds of leaf-toed geckos, genus Phyllodactylus, distributed throughout the islands, but they are some of the most secretive land vertebrates on the archipelago because of their nocturnal lifestyle. No gecko specimen was ever collected from Rábida despite the extensive collecting effort from the late 19th century until the early 20th century.The sole record of gecko presence on Rábida came from sub-fossil remains estimated at 5,700 to 8,540 years old. The authors stated that it may be possible that no gecko specimen is recorded due to insufficient collecting effort. Field guides cited that there was an undescribed and possibly extinct gecko in Rábida but without details. This led the researchers to think that the geckos were already extinct when humans arrived on the archipelago.2011 eradication of brown rats, and one gecko photographed in 2012In 2011, the Galápagos National Park and its conservation partners carried out an eradication program targeting invasive brown rats. Island Conservation, which led the effort with the park, the Charles Darwin Foundation and The Raptor Center, says a gecko long thought extinct on the island was noticed a year later. In 2012, scientists and rangers surveying the island photographed a Phyllodactylus gecko, the first live leaf-toed gecko from Rábida to be documented in published literature. The specimen itself is no longer available and cannot be found in the collections where it was said to be deposited, so its identification rests on the photographs alone. The 2019 and 2021 collections, backed by tissue samples and physical specimens, provided the confirmation. Other groups that searched for the geckos prior to and during 2011 found no geckos or any trace of geckos.Nine geckos were sampled in October 2019 and 10 were collected in August 2021The observation was confirmed through two different expeditions. In October 2019, scientists collected tail tissue from nine individuals of geckos and returned the reptiles to nature. In early August 2021, ten whole specimens were caught by hand at night, mainly among lava rocks. These geckos were deposited in the vertebrate collection of the Charles Darwin Foundation in Puerto Ayora, while tissues were sent to the zoological museum of Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador in Quito. In a combined analysis of two mitochondrial genes, the Rábida geckos fell within Phyllodactylus maresi but differed from Santiago geckos by 19 mutations. The 2025 study in PLOS ONE, led by Omar Torres-Carvajal, sequenced DNA from five of the samples. The Rábida geckos formed a strongly supported group closely related to Phyllodactylus maresi from Santiago and Marchena, and the authors assigned them to that species. Their morphology was similar to geckos from Santiago and Marchena.Because of that genetic divergence, the authors classified the Rábida geckos as a distinct evolutionary unit that can be managed separately. However, there is a warning in place. Some uncertainty remains about the classification of Phyllodactylus maresi, because few complete museum specimens exist for comparison: only five in total, with three from Santiago and none from Marchena. The ten whole specimens collected on Rábida in 2021 now add to that limited reference material. The authors indicate that the geckos from Rábida Island may have been helped by the process of rodent eradication, with increased distribution and population levels making them more visible. Lizard populations in the Caribbean, as well as those on offshore New Zealand islands, have shown signs of recovery after rodent eradications were performed. The ecological connection between rodents and geckos on Rábida Island is not known. The paper reports no population estimate, and it cannot show whether the geckos survived hidden through the rat years or recolonized. It shows that a species thought lost was present, genetically distinctive, and found after the rats were removed.Another Galápagos rediscovery, and why voucher specimens matterThe authors compare the find with other Galápagos rediscoveries. A 2022 study in Communications Biology showed that the Fernandina giant tortoise, Chelonoidis phantasticus, is not extinct. After the 2019 rediscovery, the only female found was moved to the park's tortoise center, and expeditions began searching for males. A valuable point learned from the findings of this paper is that vouchers with DNA samples are ideal for recording common and rarely studied species like the leaf-toed gecko because this will allow conservation efforts to be linked to specific interventions, such as removal of invasive species.You use AI every day. articles.title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
articles.body:
The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class.

A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".

Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.

Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality.

"You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.

There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.

The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible.

The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.

The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.

Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.

The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.

In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school.

In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.

Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching.

The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.

The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.

The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.

Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.

The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools.

Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.

The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.

Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge.

"We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.

Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago.

The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".

Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

articles.title: University of Mississippi identifies 2 students found dead in cases that raise kratom concerns
articles.summary: The University of Mississippi named two undergrads, from Colorado and Georgia, as the students found dead in cases that sparked renewed concerns about kratom.
articles.body: The University of Mississippi on Thursday named two undergrads, from Colorado and Georgia, as the students found dead earlier this week in cases that sparked renewed concerns about the drug kratom. Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, a 20-year-old junior from Atlanta, died this week, Ole Miss said. Both students were found on Monday, one on campus and the other in the city of Oxford, authorities have said. Packaged kratom was discovered during each of these separate death investigations, but no definitive link has been made between the drug and these deaths, officials said. Kratom is an herb with opioid-like effects sometimes sold at gas stations or online. It has gained popularity in the U.S. as an unapproved treatment for pain, anxiety and drug dependence. Kratom can either be stimulating or sedating, depending on the dosage taken, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. Shawnboda Mead, the vice chancellor for student affairs, urged the campus community to reserve any judgement until law enforcement finishes its probe. “We know there is heightened media attention and that you may be eager for answers. We also recognize that inaccurate information is being shared by individuals who do not have access to the facts,” Mead said in statement. “We can all help by not repeating information that has not been officially confirmed and by avoiding public speculation about what happened or why, especially as the causes of the two deaths are still under investigation.” Phi Delta Theta identified Strang as a member of its fraternity. “Out of respect for Robert, his family, and those closest to him, the Fraternity has refrained from public comment until his name was publicly released,” Phi Delta Theta said in a statement on Thursday. “The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy,” the fraternity said. “Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them.”

articles.title: Texas homeowner Elizabeth Luna wins $33,243 after nearly 3-year HOA battle over rental ban, tenant interference and blocked property sale; HOA ordered to pay $20,743, president Terri Thomure $12,500
articles.summary: A Texas homeowner has won more than $33,000 in damages, attorney’s fees and other awards after a nearly three-year legal battle with her homeowners
articles.body: A Texas homeowner has won more than $33,000 in damages, attorney’s fees and other awards after a nearly three-year legal battle with her homeowners association over rental restrictions, tenant interference and an attempt to block the sale of her property.Elizabeth Luna, who owned a rental townhome in the Oaks Northwest community near the San Antonio Medical Center, prevailed in a Bexar County court case against the HOA and its president, Terri Thomure. The case, reported by KSAT, centered on a dispute that began after the association moved to restrict short-term rentals.HOA changed rental rules after Luna bought propertyLuna purchased the townhome when there were no restrictions preventing her from renting it out, according to the report.That changed in 2023 when HOA President Terri Thomure pushed for a ban on short-term rentals in the 11-unit community. Luna challenged the change, alleging that a special meeting held in March 2023 did not comply with notice requirements under Texas law.Luna argued that the procedural issue made the amendment invalid.Despite the new restrictions, Luna said she attempted to comply with the association’s rules by securing a tenant under a 12-month lease.Tenant allegedly backed out after HOA confrontationThe dispute escalated when, according to Luna’s lawsuit, Thomure approached the tenant’s assistant in the community’s parking lot.Luna alleged that Thomure did not identify herself and demanded to know who the woman was and why she was at the property. Luna told KSAT that the interaction was unsettling and that the tenant subsequently terminated the lease.The dispute later extended to Luna’s attempt to sell the townhome.After Luna put the property on the market, the HOA filed a legal claim against the home that prevented the sale from proceeding, she told the station. A judge later dismissed the claim, allowing Luna to complete the sale in May 2024.Court orders HOA and president to payLuna continued pursuing the case even after selling the property.In May 2026, a judge in Bexar County’s 438th District Court ruled in her favor. The Oaks Northwest HOA was ordered to pay Luna $10,743.39 in damages and $10,000 in attorney’s fees, while Thomure was separately ordered to pay $12,500 for interfering with Luna’s rental contract.The combined judgments total $33,243.39.Luna told KSAT that both judgments have been paid.Luna says homeowners should hold boards accountableReflecting on the nearly three-year dispute, Luna said her goal was to demonstrate that homeowners have options when they believe an HOA board is abusing its authority or failing to follow applicable rules.“What was going through my head when all of this was happening is the abuse of power of the homeowners association,” Luna told KSAT.She said the lengthy legal fight ultimately showed her that homeowners should not be afraid to challenge decisions they believe are improper.“If you find that your board members are not following the rules, hold them accountable,” Luna said. “Hold them to a higher standard.”HOA disputes continue to draw attentionLuna’s case highlights the disputes that can arise between homeowners and associations over rental restrictions, property sales and the authority of HOA boards.HOAs can establish and enforce rules affecting properties within their communities, but their actions remain subject to governing documents and applicable state laws. In Luna’s case, the court proceedings ultimately resulted in financial judgments against both the association and its president.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: NRI man says wife in India turned into operations manager handling cook, maid and deep-cleaning service: Domestic help doesn't mean zero effort
articles.summary: An NRI man said he got a reality check about life in India when his wife spent about four months in the country before their final plan to relocate to
articles.body: An NRI man said he got a reality check about life in India when his wife spent about four months in the country before their final plan to relocate to India. While everyone claims life is easier in India because of the easy availablity of domestic help, the Redditor said it does not always make life smooth. Their random hours, unannounced leaves take a huge mental toll, the man said adding that his wife in India had to take up the domestic operations manager role, handling maids."My wife spent about four months back in India recently staying at our place, and while everyone always hype up how easy life gets with affordable domestic help, her actual experience was completely different," the Reddit post said."Having lived abroad for years where everything is DIY and automated, she was used to fixed routines. In India, within two weeks she realized she had essentially taken on a full-time operations manager role. Coordinating between a cook, a maid, and a deep-cleaning service coming in at completely random hours, handling sudden unannounced leaves, and dealing with constant friction over how things should be done took a huge mental toll," the post added."She went in thinking having help would free up her entire day, but ended up spending half her morning waiting around for people to show up or managing schedule mismatches. It was a solid reality check for both of us that having domestic help in India doesn't automatically mean zero effort—it just trades physical labor for mental management," the post said.Social media reaction to the Reddit post: 'Being a memsahib is a skill'Many Redditors could relate to the problem and agreed that managing 2-3 people is not easy as it requires a different skill set than doing everything alone. "As ridiculous as it sounds , being a "memsahib" is a skill and not everyone can do it. You often need to demonstrate a level of authority and direct management which is difficult for a lot of people who are millennials and younger," one wrote.Others dived into the technicality and one said that domestic help services in the US are costlier and hence they are very professional -- they don't need any managing. "It's the cheap labour piece that entices most people. You need to have a certain income level to have maids, nannies and personal support workers in the West. Generally any sort of customer service is abysmal in India because of the lack of training and low wages," one said."This is so true. Overseas you just put on a podcast, clean your own apartment in an hour, and move on with your day. In India, you spend half your energy managing 3 different people's schedules and temperaments. The physical labor is lower, but the mental overhead of managing people is real," another wrote.

articles.title: In 2015, a Phoenix man paid $5.99 for a LeCoultre Deep Sea Alarm at Goodwill; after experts confirmed it was authentic, he sold the rare watch days later for more than $35,000
articles.summary: An Arizona man looking for a used golf cart at a local charity shop left with a rare 1950s diving watch that earned him more than $35,000.
articles.body: An Arizona man looking for a used golf cart at a local charity shop left with a rare 1950s diving watch that earned him more than $35,000. Zach Norris bought the vintage LeCoultre Deep Sea Alarm for $5.99 after finding it face down in a basket of battery-powered watches at a Goodwill store in Phoenix. Days later, he gave the watch to a well-known collector in California and received $35,000 in cash plus his personal dream watch, an Omega Speedmaster Professional. The deal turned an ordinary thrift store trip into a life-changing windfall, giving Norris the money he needed for his upcoming wedding. According to detailed reporting by watch publication Hodinkee, Norris knew the LeCoultre name because of his interest in vintage watches. However, he initially did not realize how rare the watch was or how much it was worth.Uncovering a horological rarityThe watch Norris found in the store's bin on West Thunderbird Road was a LeCoultre Deep Sea Alarm from around 1959. Swiss company Jaeger-LeCoultre made fewer than 1,000 examples of this model for the American market. The watches were marked simply "LeCoultre" to meet United States import rules at the time. The reference 857 was also historically important because it was one of the first diving watches with an internal mechanical alarm that warned divers when it was time to return to the surface. Goodwill had priced the watch at just $5.99, placing it among ordinary discarded items. Norris bought it immediately. He told local news station KTVK that he was so careful with the watch that he hardly wanted the cashier to touch it during checkout. "Sometimes they just miss it, they don't know," Norris told KTVK, explaining how such a valuable watch ended up in a bargain bin. "It's not a very fancy-looking piece. You have to know what it is."Authenticating the bargain findingAfter taking the watch home, Norris posted photos of his $5.99 find in a vintage watch group on Facebook. The post quickly spread through the watch community and attracted interest from collectors around the world. To check whether the watch was genuine, Norris took it to Oliver Smith Jeweler, an authorized Jaeger-LeCoultre retailer in Scottsdale, Arizona. A local watchmaker opened the caseback and confirmed that it contained a genuine and clean LeCoultre K815 mechanical movement. Although the hour hand had some minor cosmetic wear, the watch still had its original, unpolished case and a well-preserved aluminum bezel. The internal alarm also still worked, vibrating and making a sound as it was designed to do. Hodinkee editor Eric Wind contacted Norris directly and advised him about the watch's real market value, helping ensure that the lucky buyer would not be taken advantage of by dealers looking for a quick profit.Closing a life changing transactionPrivate buyers quickly began making offers, but one deal stood out. Eric Ku, a well-known vintage watch dealer and collector based in California, offered Norris more than $35,000 for the watch. Ku already had a nearly perfect example of the LeCoultre Deep Sea Alarm. However, he wanted an original watch in honest condition that he could wear regularly without worrying about damaging a museum-quality example. Norris accepted the deal with two conditions. The package had to include an Omega Speedmaster Professional, and he wanted to deliver the LeCoultre himself instead of sending it through the mail. Norris flew to the San Francisco area and personally handed the watch to Ku. In return, he received the cash payment and the Omega Speedmaster. The money helped pay for his wedding to his fiancée, Leandra Knudson. Norris also gave part of his profits back to Goodwill.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rogan warns of youth support for communism as comic Yakov Smirnoff recalls escape from USSR
articles.summary: Joe Rogan slammed young Americans' growing push toward communism during a powerful conversation with Yakov Smirnoff about escaping the Soviet Union.
articles.body: Podcaster Joe Rogan blasted what he described as a "push towards communism" among young Americans as he spoke to legendary comedian Yakov Smirnoff, who grew up in the USSR. Smirnoff, a Soviet-born comedian who became popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, described to Rogan how he and his father would secretly listen to Voice of America, a U.S. government-funded international news broadcaster, late at night, knowing that they would get in trouble if anybody knew. He also described how his mother was greatly concerned over what might happen if others found out that they were yearning for America. VANCE WARNS THERE WILL BE A 'SOCIALIST PRESIDENT IN THIS COUNTRY' IF GOP DOESN'T FIX ECONOMY FOR YOUNG PEOPLE Later in life, after working aboard cruise ships, he proposed that he and his family leave the USSR and apply for a visa to the U.S., and he recalled his mother warned that they might face repercussions if they did so, warning that it would be like "you're going to go through hell." "And my dad said, ‘Yeah, we will.’ And she said, ‘Well, if you're willing to do it, so am I,'" Smirnoff recalled. Smirnoff said the process of getting a visa to America was only possible because of a deal involving the Carter administration, Soviet emigration and U.S. grain. "[Carter] wanted to see some human rights in the Soviet Union. And the Soviet leadership was — they were starving. They didn't have food. So, they needed food from America. So, Jimmy Carter made a deal that we're going to give you grain, and you allow people to get out, and that's how we were kind of exchanged for some wheat, you know," he said. "That's how we got out." "Wow. Holy s---, man … you sometimes need to be reminded how fortunate you are," Rogan said of Americans like himself. "You know, Americans in particular, we're very, you know, it's not our fault. You know, people become accustomed to where they live. … And they think this is normal, which is one of the reasons why this push towards communism amongst young people is so infuriating to me." Rogan said he understood why some people might be drawn to socialism out of a sense of "empathy" and the contrast between "people that are so rich and people that are so poor." "But the solution is not to make the government decide who gets what because they never decide the right way," he warned. "They do what people do," Rogan warned of communist officials. "What people do when they have power is they enact total control over the population so that they can maintain power, and then they live in luxury. And then you wait in line for bread, and that's how it is all over the f---ing world. "And if you step out of line, they shoot you. That's where communism goes. So, what we need is, like, a more, a more moral and ethical version of capitalism." SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM Elizabeth Pipko, a former RNC national spokesperson and the daughter of immigrants from the Soviet Union, spoke to Fox News Digital about the exchange and her family having escaped from the USSR. "I’m especially moved by his story because it is so incredibly similar to my own family’s," she said. "My grandfather told me many times about the secret radio he kept hidden inside a pillowcase, where he and my young mother would listen to Voice of America. Living in the Soviet Union, they would listen and dream of a better life, never knowing that one day America would deliver on those dreams and more. "I hope people understand that stories like this are incredibly special, but they are not unique," Pipko continued. "For generations, America has been a beacon of freedom and hope to people around the world, including millions who suffered under the horrors of communism. America has defeated communism before — both in reality and in spirit — and will continue to do so until the bitter end." "We have a duty to protect what so many came here searching for and to keep our country free from the ideology that they escaped," Pipko added. articles.title: India’s homegrown AI-powered combat aircraft hits 100-hour flight test milestone
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An Indian AI warfare company, Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA), has completed 100 cumulative hours of flight testing of its indigenous
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Indian AI warfare company, Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA), has completed 100 cumulative hours of flight testing of its indigenous FWD Kaal Bhairava Lite, an indigenous, AI-powered autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) for long-endurance intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), and tactical operations.Designed and manufactured entirely in India, with an indigenisation rate of 80%, the platform has undergone flight testing in demanding weather conditions, including 25-30 knot gusts over the Bay of Bengal, providing the development team with real-world flight data on aircraft behaviour and control in challenging wind conditions, a company statement said. It has also completed a demonstration in the challenging operating environment of J&K, supporting the platform's development for multi-terrain defence operations, it said.Built with zero foreign dependency, the platform ensures complete data sovereignty and eliminates external kill-switch risks while being positioned at a fraction of the cost of comparable Predator-class UAV systems.Suhas Tejaskanda, founder and CEO of Bengaluru-based FWDA, said, “One hundred hours of flight testing gives us an extensively tested indigenous aircraft architecture. Kaal Bhairava has demonstrated its short-field capability, strong climb performance and operation in demanding wind conditions. With a 1,200-km-class design and 8-10 hours of endurance, we believe the platform has significant potential for both the Indian Navy requirement and international markets.”The development comes as the Indian Navy examines long-range ship- and shore-launched loitering munitions, with its current RFI seeking a system with a range exceeding 1,000 km and more than nine hours of endurance.According to FWDA, the Kaal Bhairava programme is continuing to generate interest from multiple parts of India and international markets. The programme has secured a $25 million export order from a South Asian nation and enabled the company's first international manufacturing node in Portugal, marking a significant milestone in India's global expansion strategy.

articles.title: John Green just published his first novel in nearly 10 years — he leaned on these essentials while writing “Hollywood, Ending”
articles.summary: John Green just published “Hollywood, Ending,” his first novel in almost a decade. He shares what inspired the story, plus his writing and book tour essentials.
articles.body: Talking Shop is our series where we talk to interesting people about their most interesting buys. Maybe you read “The Fault in Our Stars” when it debuted as a bestseller, relied on Crash Course videos to study for college finals or subscribed to the Vlogbrothers YouTube channel after stumbling upon a few videos. However you discover John Green, it’s easy to become a fan of his work (at least in my opinion) and wonder what he’s doing next. This week, he gave us the answer. For the first time in nearly a decade, Green published a new book, his highly-anticipated novel, “Hollywood, Ending,” and he’s trying his absolute best to let you read it without spoilers. “I feel like people who read a book the week it comes out should be able to read it completely cold,” says Green, who’s been extremely careful about how he discusses “Hollywood, Ending” in interviews, on social media and on tour. He’s happy to give you a bird’s eye view of the plot, explain how he developed the characters and share where he found inspiration. But you need to crack open your copy for anything beyond that, or press play on the audiobook, which he totally supports. I recently talked to Green about writing “Hollywood, Ending,” what he needs within reach while working and his travel must-haves for book tours. He also gave me a mini tutorial on how he organizes his library, and, I promise, you’ll want to redo yours after reading his method. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Per Green’s request, I won’t spoil “Hollywood, Ending” after reading it, so here’s my one sentence synopsis: It tells the story of two young actors navigating the complexities of fame while falling in love and working on a movie together, a biopic about artist Andy Warhol. Green addresses themes in the book that he’s been ruminating on for a while. “From the time I first had books adapted to movies, I knew that Hollywood would be an interesting place to write about, and I was interested in the ways that it’s not just movie stars now who are commodifying their private experience for public consumption,” says Green. “I’ve long felt like that would be fertile ground for a novel, but it took the last eight years to really find my way through it.” “Hollywood, Ending” is technically Green’s first fiction book for an adult audience: “The Fault in Our Stars,” “Looking for Alaska,” “Turtles All the Way Down,” “Paper Towns,” “An Abundance of Katherines” and “Will Grayson, Will Grayson” all centered around teens and naturally fell into the Young Adult (YA) genre. But he told me that he approached writing for adults very similarly to how he did for teens because both groups are “intellectually sophisticated and careful readers.” “The problems the characters in this book are facing are the problems of early adulthood. When you’re in your 20s, you’re trying to figure out not just what you’re going to do with your life, but who you’re going to do life with,” says Green. “You have this huge array of possibilities for how your life can go, which is equal parts intoxicating and terrifying. I wanted to explore those problems and that time of life.” Green’s favorite place to write is in his office, which is a shed on his property in Indianapolis. “It’s quiet, it’s solitary and it suits my introverted nature,” he says. While putting pen to paper (well, fingers to keyboard), he often listens to his favorite band, The Mountain Goats, and he always has a hot cup of coffee within reach — he admittedly drinks a lot of it throughout the day, usually in his Don’t Forget to be Awesome glass mug. Green’s go-to brewer is the Moccamaster since he prefers drip coffee. And while he’s passionate about how the quality of the coffee itself matters more than the brewing method, the Moccamaster is a top notch machine that’s built to withstand constant use. The specific type of coffee Green drinks is from Keats & Co., a company he and his brother, Hank Green, founded as part of Good Store, a marketplace they run that donates 100 percent of its profits to charity. Keats & Co. came about after the Greens worked with a coffee roaster in Kansas City for a year to nail down flavor profiles for their products. “We work with small communities of farmers to get the best beans in the world, and then we work with one of the best roasters in the world to make really extraordinary coffee,” he says. “I don’t like to brag, but I do drink the coffee every day, and when I have to drink grocery store coffee, I’m kind of grossed out.” Now that “Hollywood, Ending” is published, Green is going on a 20-city book tour. “I’m traveling for like a month with a carry-on suitcase, so nothing inessential goes into it — only clothing, toothbrushes and the absolute essentials allowed,” he says. “I always travel with a book because you’re never alone in the world as long as you have a book to read.” Green’s favorite book of the year is “Canon: A Novel” by Paige Lewis — he even got to write a blurb for it that appears on the jacket. When he’s done reading his books, he finds a spot for them in his library, which is intricately organized. “One of my most prized books is the New York Public Library’s “Guide to Organizing a Home Library’,” says Green. “They have a lot of recommendations that I took, but the main one is to separate by genre as it makes sense to you, rather than as it makes sense to someone from the outside. And then with my fiction, I separate my dead authors from my living authors, so that when an author dies, I can make the somber transition.” Before Green left for his book tour, he spent time doing one of his favorite activities: making hot sauce. “I have a garden that I share with my mother, and we grow peppers and then make hot sauce from them,” he says. “From February to October, my mom and I always know what we’re doing with our spare time. We’ve made hot sauce for probably a decade now. We just like the gardening part of it, and then we give away the hot sauce for Christmas to family and friends.” Green takes his followers behind-the-scenes while making hot sauce on social media and YouTube, including how he bottles it up in glasses like these that I found from NiceBottles. But his family’s recipe is top secret, so you’ll have to find your own if you want to make something similar. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who writes our Talking Shop series, interviewing people like Paris Hilton, Maureen Kelly, Lindsay Hubbard and Chase Crawford. To write this article, I talked to author John Green about his new book, “Hollywood, Ending,” and his favorite products to use while working, traveling and spending time at home before his book tour. articles.title: Stanford apologizes saying AI-altered photo that changed student’s gender and race  violated policy
articles.summary: Stanford University said the use of artificial intelligence to alter the race and appearance of students in a promotional photo violated its policy and was “a serious error in judgment.”
articles.body: Stanford University said the use of artificial intelligence to alter the race and appearance of students in a promotional photo violated its policy and was “a serious error in judgment.” The controversy centers on an image taken of three students posing in front of Star Ginger in the university’s dining hall, according to The Stanford Review, the student-run newspaper that first reported the story. The original photo shows one female student and two male students holding their plates as they pose for the camera. The altered image shows one of the male students replaced with an AI-generated Black female student. The other two people in the altered image were made to look noticeably slimmer. The Stanford Review reported that the altered image was used by Stanford Residential & Dining Enterprises in its advertisements. Its editor-in-chief Garret Molloy, said the altered photos were placed on welcome banners around campus. Billy Ramirez, who is Hispanic, was the student who was removed from the image, according to The New York Times. “To see me erased like that so easily was kind of very upsetting,” he told the outlet. Ramirez told The Stanford Review that he initially “found it hilarious” that the school had used AI to change the photo. “But after looking at the comparison, I was also upset because I don’t agree with Stanford making those choices about how we were represented,” he said. “Seeing my identity changed and being left out of the picture made me feel, in a way, silenced and erased from a representation that was supposed to include me,” he continued. Ramirez did not immediately respond to an email Thursday seeking comment. Molloy said he believes the school was “trying to create this kind of artificial perception of diversity.” He noticed on Wednesday that the banners had been taken down. “In the past, we did that with college photographers going around campus and trying to find a diverse friend group,” he told NBC News in a phone interview on Thursday. “Those college photographers are now being replaced with AI.” The university said in a statement that the altered image violated its policy on using AI for marketing and communications. “Not only the fact that the image was altered, but the ways in which it was altered, reflect a serious error in judgment. We have apologized to the students in the photo whose images were altered or erased,” a school spokesperson said. “Quite simply, this was wrong and should never have happened.” The university said it has launched an investigation to determine what happened and “to put in place protocols to prevent it from happening again.”

articles.title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
articles.summary: Activist Daniel Thomas is charged in connection with an incident in the English Channel on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court via videolink on Friday, the force added.

Several hundred people, many wearing black, had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside.

The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".

The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

Hampshire Police earlier said an arrest had been made after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel.

Thomas, of no fixed address, was held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, "destroying ships" under the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990 and "conduct endangering ships" under the Merchant Shipping Act 1995.

The force previously said it was examining the video which had been live-streamed on Tuesday.

A French coastguard official was on board when Thomas appeared to slash at the vessel.

Some 50 migrants who had travelled in the boat from Normandy had already been transferred on to RNLI lifeboats. They were later moved on to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

articles.title: Jim Copenhaver, man shot in Trump assassination attempt, dies 2 years later
articles.summary: A man who was injured two years ago in an assassination attempt of President Donald Trump has died, according to a statement from his family on Thursday.
articles.body: A man who was injured two years ago in an assassination attempt of President Donald Trump has died, according to a statement from his family on Thursday. He was 76. Jim Copenhaver suffered what his family described as “life-altering” injuries after being shot in Butler, Pennsylvania, on July 13, 2024. He was attending a campaign rally held by Trump when a gunman named Thomas Crooks opened fire in an assassination attempt against Trump. He died on Wednesday “surrounded by his loved ones,” according to a statement from Joseph A. Feldman, an attorney representing Copenhaver’s family. The statement did not provide a cause of death. Serving his country was a “defining” aspect of Copenhaver’s life, his family said, and he was deeply grateful for the outpouring of love he received following the Butler shooting. “As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered,” the statement said. “James was a true American patriot who believed deeply in the freedoms and ideals upon which this nation was founded, and he embodied the very best traits of our great nation.” The family released a statement through a spokesperson for Allegheny Health Network after Copenhaver at the time he was discharged. They thanked the public for their support as the family dealt with the aftermath of the “horrible, senseless, and unnecessary act of violence.” Copenhaver was hit once in the tricep while another bullet hit his abdomen, leaving him with nerve damage and required doctors to transect some of his colon. Months later, he told NBC News he lost 30 pounds and had to walk with a cane. He hadn’t even realized he was shot until he saw part of his sleeve “go away.” “I mean I heard it distinctly,” Copenhaver said of the shooting. “I turn around to my friend and I said, ‘I think I was shot.’ And that’s when I got the second one.” Former fire chief Corey Comperatore died in the shooting and Copenhaver was one of two people injured in the attack. Trump’s ear was hit by either a bullet or a fragment, but was not seriously injured, the FBI said. Crooks, 20, was shot and killed by a Secret Service sharpshooter. A motive was never uncovered in the shooting even after law enforcement officials interviewed Crooks’ relatives, neighbors, teachers and classmates. The official X account for the House Republicans posted about Copenhaver’s death, expressing the GOP’s condolences to his family. “Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance,” the post said. “We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time. May he rest in peace.”

articles.title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military actions in Middle East in UN speech
articles.summary: Dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took the podium, with the Israeli leader labelling them "moral cowards".
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly.

After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."

In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."

The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".

He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.

Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.

The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because had been denied a US entry visa.

Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him.

"They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.

He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.

Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".

New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader.

"Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.

In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".

Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February.

"Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.

A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning actress Hannah Einbinder.

The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages.

During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide.

Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence.

On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran.

Iran retaliated by carrying out missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.
